The frost does not arrive all at once; it tests the grass first, like an animal putting a single paw into cold water. 

Julian woke to the iron crack of the floorboards under his wool socks. In November, the farmhouse contracted, its beams pulling in their shoulders against the valley draft. Downstairs, the cast-iron stove sat in the kitchen corner, round-bellied and cold, holding yesterday’s gray ash in its teeth. He did not light a lamp yet. He knew the house by the geometry of its shadows—the pitch of the doorframe where his shoulder brushed when he was twenty, thirty, sixty; the low sag of the dry sink; the copper kettle catching the pale, greasy smear of dawn through the eastern windowpane.

Outside, the orchard waited on the northern slope. 

People who do not grow fruit believe an orchard is a passive thing, a field where trees merely stand until August makes them sweet. They do not know about the warfare of sap, the blind persistence of rootstocks pushing through shale, or the long, mute patience of winter. Julian pulled on his heavy canvas coat, stiff with dried mud and the brown tannin stains of cider presses from three seasons ago. He pushed his thumbs into split leather gloves and stepped onto the porch.

The air smelled of cured grass, wet shale, and woodsmoke from the chimney down in the hollow where the Miller boy was burning green birch. It was an offensive smell, green birch—bitter, full of hiss and water—the fire of a young man who hadn't cut his cordwood before the summer solstice. Julian let the screen door click shut behind him with its tinny, familiar rattle.

There were sixty-two trees left. Forty years ago, when he and Clara bought the slope, there were two hundred, mostly Baldwins and Northern Spies planted before the First World War. Time had hollowed them out from the heartwood. Wind took some; crown rot took others; lightning cleaved the grand old Russet near the stonewall in the summer of the drought. What remained were the stubborn ones, along with the forty grafts Julian had set into wild stock with his own clasp knife: *Esopus Spitzenburg*, *Ashmead’s Kernel*, *Black Oxford*, *Pitmaston Pineapple*. 

Names like incantations. Names from a century that did not require every fruit to look like a red billiard ball or endure three weeks in the refrigerated hold of a container ship. 

He walked between the rows. His boots made a dry, breaking sound in the rime. The leaves had mostly fallen now, curled into brittle copper spoons upon the earth, but here and there an apple clung to a bare spur high in the canopy. The waxwings and cedar birds had pecked the highest ones; yellow jackets had hollowed the windfalls down to parchment skins. 

He stopped by the *Black Oxford*. It was a dark, round thing, its skin the color of an old bruise, dusted with a pale violet bloom that wiped off under a thumb. It was an apple meant for late winter, so hard when picked in October that it would crack a tooth, but down in the earthen root cellar, wrapped in greaseproof paper and laid on pine slats, it would relent by February. It would soften into something aromatic and dense, tasting faintly of flint and elderberry wine.

Julian reached up and took one of the last hangers. The stem resisted, then snapped cleanly at the abscission layer. The wood did not want to surrender it, but it had no choice. That was the contract between the spur and the frost.

He held the fruit in his palm. It was freezing to the touch, heavy as a stone retrieved from a creek bed. 

He thought of Clara’s hands, which had been broader than his, with squared-off nails permanently yellowed around the cuticles from sorting fruit in the damp grading shed. She had possessed an uncanny sense for decay. She could walk down a row of bushel baskets and plunge her hand directly into the center of one, unerringly lifting out the single apple whose core had gone brown before the skin showed a mark. *It gives off a fever,* she would say, her sleeve pushed up above the elbow. *Rot runs hotter than soundness.*

She had been gone four years now, but the orchard had not become a monument to her. An orchard is too hungry to serve as a graveyard; it demands lime; it demands pruning shears; it demands that you cut away half of what grew last summer so that the sunlight can reach the interior wood in July. Grief, Julian had learned, was not a stone you laid upon the chest. It was a chore you did with cold water before the light came up. It was hauling bucket after bucket to trees whose taproots were already drinking from deep, unreachable veins.

He walked to the crest of the knoll where the stonewall crumbled into the hemlocks. Below him, the valley was filling with morning mist, white as sheep’s wool, blanketing the macadam road, the county barns, the silver silos of the dairy farm. Only the ridge-poles of the world stood clear, floating like dark islands in a lake of steam.

Julian took his clasp knife from his pocket, wiped the carbon blade against his thigh, and cut a wedge from the *Black Oxford*. The flesh was greenish-white, beaded with tiny beads of moisture that did not run. He put it in his mouth.

The bite was loud in the silence of the hill. It tasted of cold cellars, dried thyme, and iron. It was not sweet—not yet—but the acid made the back of his jaw ache with an old, sharp vitality. 

He chewed slowly, watching the mist begin to churn as the sun finally cleared the ridge, spilling thin, yellow light across the orchard floor. In twenty years, nobody would know the difference between an *Oxford* and a *Gala*. The trees would grow feral, their water sprouts shooting straight up into the air like brooms, the fruit shrinking to the size of walnuts, sour and speckled with scab. The forest would creep out from the hemlock line, first the sumac, then the birch, then the oak, until the straight lines of the rows vanished beneath the chaotic tangle of the woods.

Julian swallowed the slice. He wiped the knife against his trousers, folded the blade shut until it gave its solid, metallic snap, and put it back in his pocket. 

There was still an hour before the ground softened into mud. He had two rows left to paint with white lime against the sun-scald, to keep the bark from splitting when the February days grew warm and the February nights dropped back to zero. A man does not keep sixty trees because he expects the world to thank him for his cider. He keeps them because the ground was cleared by someone else, and to abandon a cleared field before your knees give out is a species of impoliteness.

He turned back toward the shed, the single cold apple resting quietly in his coat pocket, knocking against his hip at every step.
